first.rationale:
The two internal declines (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are causally linked: onboarding sits upstream of activation, so repairing it is the highest-leverage single slot and is the only candidate that plausibly moves both metrics. I am deliberately not taking promotional_pricing despite it being the loudest signal (competitor entry pricing): memory_73's summary records acquisition and revenue lift, not retention or margin over time, and discount-acquired price-sensitive SMB cohorts are exactly the population most likely to churn or resist re-pricing. That would trade sustainable qualified revenue for a quarter of gross adds. Referral incentives (memory_57) and enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) address neither observed decline.

I am verifying the three memories my choice actually rests on rather than the one I'm declining. The critical worry is that these are consolidated summaries whose stated outcomes are all activation/engagement metrics, with no downstream revenue-quality measure surviving consolidation. memory_31 specifically says the lift came from cutting required signup fields — those fields are often the qualification and routing data that determine whether an activated account ever becomes qualified revenue. So the recorded win may be a metric that is upstream of my objective but partly in tension with it. If the archived record for memory_31 shows the lift was measured only to first-week activation, or shows lead quality degraded, I switch to activation_messaging (memory_91), which lifts the same funnel stage without stripping qualification data. I also want to know whether memory_86 and memory_31 are two independent findings or one experiment consolidated twice, since that would mean my evidence base is thinner than it looks.

Scale is a small guarded test rather than a broad rollout: the prior evidence is real but measured on the wrong outcome for this objective, and the change touches lead qualification. Instrument it to qualified-pipeline and 90-day retention, not completion rate, and hold back the fields that drive routing. Losing the slot is cheaper than baking a bad signup schema into the funnel.

final.rationale:
Verification largely resolved my main worry. exp_31 and exp_86 are two distinct experiments, not one summary counted twice, so the evidence base is thicker than I feared. Critically, exp_86 (shortened onboarding) carries 30-day retention +3% and time-to-value -2.1 days — the recorded win is not a pure funnel-metric artifact, and the downstream indicator moves the right way. exp_31 showed my specific concern was real but small: cutting signup fields cost -1% on 30-day retention while still delivering qualified revenue +4%, so the qualification-data tradeoff exists but did not invert the objective.

I am running simplify_onboarding, weighted toward the exp_86 flow-shortening intervention rather than the exp_31 field-stripping intervention. That distinction matters: exp_86 is the one that directly targets the observed -4% onboarding completion decline, is the one with positive retention, and does not remove the routing/qualification fields that turn an activated account into qualified revenue. Onboarding sits upstream of activation, so this is the only single slot that plausibly addresses both the -4% completion and the -6% activation decline; activation_messaging (exp_91, activation +6%, retention +1%) is a genuine fallback but treats the downstream symptom while leaving the upstream leak open.

Still declining promotional_pricing despite the competitor being the loudest stimulus. memory_73 remains unverified — I spent the budget on what I intended to do rather than what I intended to refuse — and its recorded outcome is acquisition and revenue lift with no retention or margin measure surviving consolidation. Discount-acquired price-sensitive SMB is precisely the cohort most likely to churn or resist re-pricing, so it trades sustainable qualified revenue for gross adds. Referral (memory_57) and enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) address neither observed decline.

Residual uncertainty I am carrying, not resolving: exp_86 never measured qualified revenue at all, only retention as a proxy, so my primary objective is inferred rather than demonstrated for this specific intervention. exp_31's conclusion explicitly says it did not replicate outside SMB. Scale is a standard experiment rather than broad rollout on that basis. Instrument to qualified pipeline and 90-day retention as primary, completion rate as diagnostic only, hold qualification/routing fields intact, and segment SMB versus other so I learn whether the non-replication in exp_31 also applies to flow-shortening.
